query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporation of 0.5 wt.% Y₂O₃ nanoparticles into a single-phase Ti–Ni HEA will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties by providing dispersion strengthening and grain refinement.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase Ti–Ni based high-entropy alloy with an FCC structure and no secondary precipitation.
generation.intervention: Uniformly incorporate 0.5 wt.% nano-scale Y₂O₃ particles via powder decoration (e.g., using resonant acoustic mixing) before consolidation with techniques such as laser powder bed fusion or spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing conducted in an inert atmosphere between 800–1000 °C under both tensile and creep loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain refinement yielding a more uniform and reduced grain size, combined with a stable, uniformly dispersed population of Y₂O₃ nanoparticles within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Y₂O₃ nanoparticles serve as dispersion-strengthening agents by impeding dislocation motion and pinning grain boundaries, thereby increasing the yield strength and improving creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile yield strength by approximately 20–30% and improved creep life and ductility relative to the baseline alloy processed without Y₂O₃ addition.
generation.baseline: The identical Ti–Ni HEA produced without any Y₂O₃ nanoparticle incorporation.
generation.boundary: Applicable for Ti–Ni-rich single-phase alloys produced under conditions avoiding secondary phase formation; mechanical property improvements are expected in the temperature range of 800–1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements are anticipated, the exact magnitude depends on the uniform dispersion of Y₂O₃ and assurance via thermodynamic analysis that the nanoparticles remain inert in the Ti–Ni matrix at high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Ti–Ni HEA – one with the 0.5 wt.% Y₂O₃ addition (via powder decoration) and one without. Characterize nanoparticle dispersion and grain size using SEM/TEM, then subject both batches to high-temperature tensile and creep tests at 900 °C.
measurements: Grain size distribution and nanoparticle dispersion uniformity (SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y₂O₃-added alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% improvement in yield strength or creep life compared to the baseline, or if adverse reactions form between Y₂O₃ and the matrix, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A new precipitation strengthening NiCoCr-based superalloy with favorable mechanical performance and corrosion resistance was designed for ultra-supercritical power generation equipment. The degradation of mechanical properties and steam corrosion at high temperatures put forward higher requirements for alternative alloy materials; however, when the superalloy is processed to form complex shaped components through advanced additive manufacturing techniques such as laser metal deposition (LMD), hot cracks are prone to appear. This study proposed that microcracks in LMD alloys could be alleviated with powder decorated by Y2O3 nanoparticles. The results show that adding 0.5 wt.% Y2O3 can refine grains significantly. The increase in grain boundaries makes the residual thermal stress more uniform to reduces the risk of hot cracking. In addition, the addition of Y2O3 nanoparticles enhanced the ultimate tensile strength of the superalloy at room temperature by 18.3% compared to original superalloy. The corrosion resistance was also improved with 0.5 wt.% Y2O3, which was attributed to the reduction of defects and the addition of inert nanoparticles.

Additive manufacturing currently facilitates new avenues for materials discovery that have not been fully explored. In this study we reveal how additive manufacturing can be leveraged to produce dispersion strengthened (DS), multi-principal element alloys (MPEA) without the use of traditional mechanical alloying or chemical reactions. This new processing technique employed resonant acoustic mixing to coat an equiatomic NiCoCr powder with nano-scale yttrium oxides. Then, through laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), the coated powder was successfully consolidated into 99.9% dense parts. Microstructural analysis confirmed the successful incorporation and dispersion of nano-scale oxides throughout the build volume. Furthermore, high temperature mechanical testing of the DS alloys showed significant improvements in strength and ductility over the baseline NiCoCr. As a result, this recently discovered processing route opens a new alloy design and production path that is synergistic between additive manufacturing and dispersion strengthening, possibly enabling a new generation of high-performance alloys.

open_questions: How will a single-phase, titanium- and nickel-rich high-entropy alloy perform at elevated temperatures in the absence of conventional precipitate (γ′) strengthening?
Can the addition of nano-scale oxide dispersions (e.g., Y₂O₃) effectively enhance the high-temperature mechanical performance in a Ti–Ni based single-phase alloy?
What processing conditions (e.g., annealing treatments) are optimal to introduce beneficial grain refinement without inducing unwanted secondary phases?

directions.assessment: Adding a minor fraction of nano-scale oxides (e.g., ~0.5 wt.% Y₂O₃) to the single‐phase Ti–Ni HEA appears to be very promising for enhancing high‐temperature yield strength and ductility by refining the grain structure and impeding dislocation motion. The mechanism is well supported by previous studies on NiCoCr-based alloys and dispersion‐strengthened multi-principal element alloys (e.g., PMC10222657, PMC7296023). The approach is directly targeted at alleviating the high-temperature performance limitation.

directions.direction: Controlled rapid annealing to induce nanoscale ordering
directions.assessment: A rapid, high-temperature annealing treatment may trigger slight ordering (e.g., nanometric ordering fluctuations) while retaining the overall single-phase state. This could subtly enhance dislocation resistance via short-range order. However, care must be taken that additional secondary phases do not form. The mechanism is plausible but less directly verified in Ti–Ni systems.

Employing high-energy ball milling prior to consolidation (e.g., spark plasma sintering) can further refine the grain size of the single-phase alloy. Enhanced grain boundary strengthening would improve the yield strength at elevated temperatures. The approach is straightforward and supports basic strengthening physics, although the magnitude might be smaller than dispersion strengthening.

directions.direction: Minor alloying addition for enhanced solid solution strengthening
directions.assessment: Incorporating a very small amount (∼1 at.%) of an element such as Nb could improve high-temperature strength by increasing solid solution and edge-dislocation mechanisms without provoking phase separation. The supporting evidence in multicomponent alloys makes this approach plausible; however, it modifies the chemistry slightly away from the pure Ti–Ni basis.

Applying a high-temperature oxidation‐resistant coating may protect against environmental degradation and indirectly support better mechanical performance in extreme environments. Nonetheless, while useful for corrosion/oxidation, it does not directly enhance the intrinsic mechanical yield strength of the bulk alloy.

candidates.changes: Clarified the need to monitor grain coarsening during high-temperature exposure and included a requirement for literature support and additional thermal stability testing of the refined structure.

candidates.hypothesis: A rapid, high-temperature annealing treatment of a single-phase Ti–Ni HEA will induce controlled nanoscale ordering fluctuations that impede dislocation motion, thereby enhancing high-temperature strength.
candidates.intervention: Apply a short-duration annealing treatment (10–20 minutes) at a high temperature just below the melting point (approximately 0.85–0.90 Tm) of the alloy, followed by rapid quenching.
candidates.changes: Expanded the explanation on the mechanism of short-range (nanoscale) ordering induced by rapid annealing, and stressed the importance of optimizing the annealing time–temperature parameters to avoid excessive ordering or secondary phase formation.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporation of 0.5 wt.% Y₂O₃ nanoparticles into a single-phase Ti–Ni HEA will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties by providing dispersion strengthening and grain refinement.
candidates.intervention: Uniformly incorporate 0.5 wt.% nano-scale Y₂O₃ particles via powder decoration (e.g., by resonant acoustic mixing) before consolidation using techniques such as laser powder bed fusion or spark plasma sintering.
candidates.changes: Emphasized the need for thermodynamic analysis and experimental verification to confirm that Y₂O₃ nanoparticles remain stable and do not react adversely with the Ti–Ni matrix at high temperatures. Clarified dispersion uniformity requirements.
